title: How do you stay calm when nerves hit in a case interview?
description: Practical, kind advice for staying calm before and during a case interview, and what to do in the moment when your mind goes blank.
hook: You stay calm in a case interview by making the format familiar through lots of spoken practice, rehearsing how you recover when you get stuck, and having a simple routine for the moment nerves hit: pause, go back to the goal, and say what you know. Almost everyone is nervous before a case, and it is not a sign you are unprepared. The aim is not to feel nothing; it is to have a few tools ready so nerves do not take over.

Why nerves are normal

A case interview combines several things that make most people anxious: being judged, doing maths aloud, and not knowing what comes next. A racing heart and a dry mouth are your body getting ready, and a little of that sharpens focus. Trouble starts when nerves crowd out your thinking. The tools below are about keeping enough calm to think, not about removing nerves altogether.

Before the day

Practise out loud, with people

Nerves fade with familiarity. The first live case with a partner feels strange; by the tenth, the format itself stops being frightening and you can spend your attention on the problem. Silent practice from a book does not build this, so do most of your cases aloud with another person. The guide to practising with a partner shows how to set it up.

Practise recovering, not just succeeding

If every practice case goes smoothly, the first curveball in a real interview will feel like a disaster. Ask partners to throw you a surprise sometimes: a contradictory fact, a messy chart, a hard follow-up. Getting stuck should become familiar too.

Sleep beats cramming

A rested brain does maths and structures far better than a tired one with one extra framework in it. Stop preparing at a sensible time the night before.

On the day

  • Warm up, gently. Use a short 30-minute warm-up: something familiar to read, a voice warm-up and one easy mini-case.
  • Breathe slowly. Breathing in for four counts and out for six, a few times, calms many people quickly. A longer out-breath is the part that matters.
  • Reframe the interviewer. They are not trying to catch you out. They have a role to fill and are hoping you are the person who fills it.
  • Write the goal at the top of your page. It becomes your anchor if you lose your way.

When your mind goes blank

It happens to strong candidates too. What matters is what you do next. Use three steps:

  1. Ask for a moment. "Could I take a few seconds to think about that?" Nobody minds.
  2. Go back to the goal. Look at the box at the top of your notes. What is the client trying to achieve?
  3. Say what you know. "So far we know A and B. We're trying to get to C. So the next thing to check is..." Saying it out loud often gives you the next step.

The third step works because it turns a blank into a summary, and a summary is a perfectly good thing to be saying while your brain catches up.

When you make a mistake: a worked example

Suppose a client sold 50,000 units at $40 last year, which is $2.0M of revenue. This year it sold 46,000 units at $38. You quickly multiply last year's volume by this year's price, get 50,000 × $38 = $1.9M, and tell the interviewer revenue fell 5%. The interviewer says: "Are you sure about the volume?"

A weak response defends the number out of embarrassment, or apologises at length and loses the thread.

A strong response sounds like this:

You're right, I used last year's volume with this year's price. Correcting it: 46,000 times $38 is $1.748M, so revenue fell from $2.0M to about $1.75M, a 12.6% drop, not 5%. That's bigger than I said, and it comes from both sides: volume is down 8% and price is down 5%. So we need to look at both.

Check it: 46,000 ÷ 50,000 = 0.92 and $38 ÷ $40 = 0.95; 0.92 × 0.95 = 0.874, so revenue is 87.4% of last year, a 12.6% fall. The candidate corrected once, recalculated out loud, and said what the correction changes. That kind of calm correction is exactly the judgement a case is designed to test.

Silence that helps and silence that hurts

There is a difference between silence while thinking and silence because you are lost. The first is fine: ask for a moment before structuring or before a calculation, then come back with your headline first. The second is the one to avoid. If you are stuck for more than about 20 seconds, start talking through what you know using the three steps above. If you genuinely cannot reconcile two numbers, name the discrepancy and ask which definition is right: "I'm getting two different figures for the market. Is this one by value and that one by volume?" Nobody expects a flawless recital; the interview tests how you work through uncertainty.

Build recovery into your practice

  • Ask a partner to interrupt once per case with a contradictory fact.
  • Give yourself ten seconds to look at the objective, restate what is known and propose the next test.
  • Practise the correction script: "Sorry, I made an error there. It's $2.4M, not $24M, which changes the conclusion to..."

Repeat this until a correction no longer feels like the end of the case. If you are playing interviewer for a friend, the interviewer mode gives you the facts to drop in when they ask.

After the interview

Write down what went well and one thing to improve, then let it go. Replaying it all evening does not change the outcome, and you may have another interview tomorrow. If the news is bad, read what to do after a rejection.

Common mistakes

  • Rushing to fill silence. Talking fast to avoid a pause makes errors more likely. Pause, then speak.
  • Hiding a mistake. Hoping the interviewer missed it rarely works. Correct it yourself, out loud.
  • Letting one stumble sink the case. A bad calculation in minute 10 does not decide the result. Reset and keep going.
  • Cramming the night before. It costs sleep and adds anxiety.

Practise it

1. Mid-case, you realise you have forgotten what the client asked. What do you say?

Show the answer

Look at the goal you wrote at the top of your page. If you did not write it, be honest: "Let me make sure I'm still answering the right question. The goal is to restore profit to last year's level, correct?" Interviewers prefer a quick check to a wrong turn.

2. You say a market is worth $24M, then realise it is $2.4M. Write the one-sentence correction.

Show the answer

"Sorry, I slipped a zero: it's $2.4M, not $24M, which means the market is too small to justify a new factory on its own." Correct once, then say what it changes.

3. The interviewer asks a question and your mind goes blank. Say out loud what you would do in the next 15 seconds.

Show the answer

"Could I take a moment?" Then, after a few seconds: "So far we know costs rose 10% and revenue was flat. We're trying to get profit back to $5M. So the next thing I'd look at is which cost lines grew." Ask, go back to the goal, say what you know.

Where to practise next

Read how to come across as clear and calm for the delivery habits that go with these tools, and set up regular live cases with a partner so the format becomes familiar.
